rationale: Constellation shows pure-graphite FE hotspot is flat across 10/20/30 mm (325/325/325 K, each ~15 K under the 340 K THERM-R2 limit) while mass scales linearly with thickness (18/36/54 kg/m2). Graphite also has the best conductivity-to-density ratio of the catalogued materials (150/1800=0.083 vs aluminium 200/2700=0.074, aluminium_nitride 170/3260=0.052, copper 400/8960=0.045), so it is the best mass candidate per unit thermal performance. The current lightest all-PASS design is 10 mm graphite at 18 kg/m2; this probes whether the observed thickness-flatness of the FE hotspot extends down to 1 mm, which would cut mass to ~1.8 kg/m2. Screen (R1) gets easier, not harder, as thickness drops (403/407/410 K for graphite at 10/20/30 mm, i.e. thinner is cooler under the pessimistic no-spreading model), so this candidate is expected to clear R1 comfortably; screening here is to obtain the exact mass/thickness verdicts before committing transport budget.

Same reasoning as the 1 mm graphite candidate: probes the thin end of the thickness range where FE hotspot behavior is untested on record (only 10/20/30 mm graphite exist, all at 325 K). Mass at 2 mm would be 3.6 kg/m2, far below the 18 kg/m2 record-holder.
Fills the low end of a spread across 1-9 mm graphite to locate where (if anywhere) the FE hotspot departs from the flat ~325 K seen at 10-30 mm. Mass at 3 mm would be 5.4 kg/m2.
Part of the same 1-9 mm graphite spread bracketing the untested region below the 10 mm record point (325 K FE hotspot, 18 kg/m2). Mass at 4 mm would be 7.2 kg/m2.
Midpoint of the 1-9 mm graphite spread. If the flatness seen across 10/20/30 mm (325 K throughout) holds down to 5 mm, mass would fall to 9 kg/m2, half the current lightest all-PASS design.
Part of the 1-9 mm graphite spread used to bracket the thickness at which FE hotspot may start rising above the flat ~325 K observed at 10-30 mm. Mass at 6 mm would be 10.8 kg/m2.
Part of the 1-9 mm graphite spread, closer to the known-good 10 mm point (325 K, 18 kg/m2) to help interpolate the trend. Mass at 7 mm would be 12.6 kg/m2.
Part of the 1-9 mm graphite spread, immediately below the known-good 10 mm point, to check how close to that record the flat FE behavior persists. Mass at 8 mm would be 14.4 kg/m2.

Closest untested point to the 10 mm graphite record (325 K FE, 18 kg/m2, worst margin 3). If FE hotspot is still ~325 K at 9 mm, mass drops to 16.2 kg/m2, a small but direct improvement over the current lightest all-PASS design with minimal extrapolation risk.

Cross-check backup material at a thin gauge, in case graphite's apparent thickness-flatness breaks down before aluminium's does. Aluminium has the second-best conductivity-to-density ratio (200/2700=0.074) and its FE hotspot on record is also flat across 10/20/30 mm (324/324/324 K, ~16 K margin), slightly more margin than graphite's ~15 K at 10 mm. Mass at 5 mm would be 13.5 kg/m2, still under the current 18 kg/m2 record if it holds.

Bracketing the untested 1-9mm graphite range with an even spread to find where, if anywhere, the FE hotspot departs from the flat ~325K seen at 10/20/30mm pure-graphite designs on record, before spending further budget refining any PASS/FAIL boundary. Round-2 result on record shows a sharp break between 1mm graphite (FE 344K, FAIL by 4.44K) and 3mm graphite (FE 331K, PASS by 8.63K), unlike the mild ~1-2K/mm drift seen from 3mm up to 9mm (331->328->326->326K). This is a surprise relative to the flat 322-325K trend at 10-30mm that motivated this batch; the flatness clearly breaks down below ~3mm as spreading resistance grows sharply at low thickness. Transporting 2mm graphite (already screened, R1 401K/R3 3.6kg/R4 0.2cm all pass with large margins) to pin down exactly where the PASS/FAIL boundary sits between the known 1mm-fail and 3mm-pass points, since whole-mm resolution means this is the last point needed to resolve the boundary exactly.

Transported results now on record show 1mm graphite FAILS THERM-R2 (344K, over by 4.44K) while 2mm graphite PASSES (335K, margin 4.69K) -- the thin-plate hotspot is spreading-resistance dominated and rises sharply below ~2-3mm, unlike the flat 322-325K seen at 10-30mm. At fixed thickness, higher conductivity gives a lower hotspot (10mm data: copper k=400 -> 322K < aluminium k=200 -> 324K < graphite k=150 -> 325K), so aluminium's higher conductivity than graphite (200 vs 150 W/mK) should reduce the thin-plate spreading penalty relative to graphite at the same 1mm thickness. Aluminium's density (2700 kg/m3) is low enough that 1mm of it (2.7 kg/m2) would still be lighter than the current lightest all-PASS design (2mm graphite, 3.6 kg/m2) if it passes. Since 1mm is the thinnest whole-mm layer possible and graphite (the only lighter-density catalogued material) already fails at 1mm, a passing 1mm aluminium design cannot be beaten in mass by any other single- or multi-layer combination from this material set.

Second candidate at the minimum 1mm thickness, run alongside 1mm aluminium to bracket the material trend in case aluminium narrowly fails. Aluminium_nitride's conductivity (170 W/mK) sits between graphite's (150, fails at 1mm/344K) and aluminium's (200, untested at 1mm), so its thin-plate hotspot should fall between theirs. Its density (3260 kg/m3) gives 1mm a mass of 3.26 kg/m2, still lighter than the current lightest all-PASS design (2mm graphite, 3.6 kg/m2), so a PASS here would also be an improvement even if not as good as aluminium.

Testing the two lightest untested candidates at the minimum 1mm thickness together to bracket the material trend efficiently. Graphite (lowest density, 1800) fails at 1mm (344K); aluminium (2700, k=200) and aluminium_nitride (3260, k=170) are the next-lightest catalogued materials and both would beat the current lightest all-PASS design (2mm graphite, 3.6 kg/m2) if either passes, at 2.7 and 3.26 kg/m2 respectively. Since 1mm is the thinnest whole-mm layer allowed and no material lighter than graphite exists in the table (epoxy's 0.2 W/mK conductivity is a near-insulator, not a credible candidate), a PASS on aluminium at 1mm would be provably the lightest possible design from this material set.

Epoxy (1200 kg/m3) is the only catalogued material lighter than graphite (1800 kg/m3), so a 1mm graphite + 1mm epoxy stack would mass 3.0 kg/m2 -- lighter than the current lightest all-PASS design (2mm graphite, 3.6 kg/m2) -- if it passes THERM-R2. Graphite is placed at the heated face (per the layer ordering convention, source outward) so it does the spreading work first, as it does when alone; epoxy is placed outward. This is a deliberately marginal/high-risk probe: the record shows pure-graphite FE hotspot is highly sensitive to how much conductive thickness is present close to and behind the source (344K at 1mm vs 335K at 2mm, a 9K swing for 1mm of added graphite), which is evidence that outward material does real thermal work here (most likely because convective cooling sits beyond the outward face, so heat must conduct through the full stack to reach it). Substituting epoxy (k=0.2 W/mK, ~750x worse than graphite's 150) for the second mm therefore seems likely to perform worse than 1mm graphite alone (344K, already a 4.44K fail) rather than better, since it adds series resistance instead of conductive spreading volume. Testing it directly rather than assuming, per the instruction to adjust to results rather than argue with them -- and because a pass would be a meaningful further mass win, cheap to check against the ample remaining budget.
